memory_update.text: Add DLR and EQIX as direct data-center asset-owner/platform candidates for the AI/electrification load-growth node; they convert AI compute demand into powered-capacity demand.
Add Dominion Energy as a regulated-utility candidate because Virginia data-center growth creates direct load, grid-connection, and capex-recovery exposure.
Add Vistra as a firm-power/dispatchable-generation candidate, but retain inference status until signed data-center PPAs or large-load contracts are verified.
Add IES Holdings as a second-order electrical/technology infrastructure contractor with explicit data-center end-market exposure.

Future passes should separately map transformer/switchgear suppliers, backup-generation vendors, utility-scale gas turbine suppliers, grid software/forecasting vendors, and regional utilities in ERCOT/PJM/MISO/SERC with large-load tariff filings.

Add POWL as a focused U.S.-listed medium-voltage switchgear/custom power-distribution candidate for AI/data-center power-delivery bottlenecks; strongest evidence is the >$400M data-center order and $1.8B backlog disclosed in May 2026.
Add HUBB as a grid-infrastructure and electrical-solutions supplier linked to load growth, utility T&D, transmission/substation demand, and datacenter projects.
Add NVT as an electrical connection/protection and data-center infrastructure component supplier with explicit 2026 strategy emphasis on AI-related data centers and power utilities.
Add FIX as a mission-critical mechanical/electrical contracting capacity candidate; backlog is very large, but data-center revenue mix needs stronger primary-source quantification.

Add STRL as a site-development plus electrical/mechanical services provider for data-center and mission-critical campuses; Q1 2026 materials show data centers/semis/manufacturing dominate E-Infrastructure backlog.

For the AI/electrification load-growth node, the investable chokepoint appears to migrate from generic electricity demand toward power-ready sites, switchgear, substations, grid T&D components, and scarce electrical/mechanical execution capacity.

Need a separate pass on transformer manufacturers, copper/wire/cable suppliers, backup/on-site generation, batteries/UPS, grid-interconnection software, and regulated utilities with the largest signed large-load agreements.

POWL should be tracked as a high-relevance small/mid-cap electrical infrastructure chokepoint: custom switchgear, power control rooms, utility/data-center power distribution, and recent large data-center order evidence.

FIX and EME expand the universe beyond OEMs into specialty electrical/mechanical construction labor and project execution, a likely gating factor when data-center power campuses move from permits to buildout.
HUBB maps the node to grid hardware and substation/T&D capacity rather than only data-center interior equipment.
CMI adds mission-critical backup and power-generation exposure; compare with CAT in a separate pass because CAT has also become a visible data-center power-generation beneficiary.
Follow-up screen should test ITRI, NVT, ATKR, MTZ, WWD, CAT, and data-center REITs/utilities with specific revenue/backlog evidence rather than ticker-memory assumptions.

node: AI/data-center and broad electrification load growth
summary: Combined focused Layer 1B searches: Expanded the universe for the demand-side node by adding five US-listed companies with direct exposure to AI/data-center load growth or the power/interconnection bottleneck around that load. The additions emphasize data-center asset owners with secured capacity, a Virginia utility exposed to the largest US data-center cluster, a dispatchable power generator likely exposed to large-load procurement, and an electrical/technology contractor with explicit data-center end-market exposure. This is research support only, not a buy/sell recommendation. Expanded the universe around the demand node into U.S.-listed companies that sell scarce electrical gear, power-connection/protection products, mission-critical construction, or integrated site/electrical services required before AI/data-center loads can interconnect reliably. This is research support only, not a buy/sell list. The strongest chokepoint evidence in this pass is concentrated in medium-voltage switchgear, grid/substation/transmission products, electrical connections/protection, and contractor capacity for mission-critical campuses. Expanded the universe around the AI/data-center load-growth node toward second-order chokepoints: electrical construction labor, custom switchgear/power distribution, utility grid hardware, backup/on-site power generation, and grid-edge software. The strongest candidates in this pass are companies whose revenues or backlog are already tied to data-center, utility, substation, or mission-critical power demand rather than only broad AI compute spending.
